title: Navigating by Gravity Alone
hook: A ship crossed 83 km of open water with GPS switched off, steering by tiny local changes in Earth's gravity measured with falling cold atoms.
key_points: Satellite navigation is jammed or unavailable at sea, and pure inertial navigation drifts without an external fix.
Gravity map matching is a passive alternative: measure local gravity, compare it to a known anomaly map, infer where you are.
The team flew an atom-interferometer gravimeter on a 29 m vessel in an unstabilised cabin, hybridised with a classical accelerometer.
Over an 83 km trajectory with GNSS excluded, gravity aiding bounded the inertial drift at nautical-mile-level accuracy.
In survey mode it resolved features down to ~300 m along track, about 50x finer than the satellite gravity map.
A 56-hour stationary test showed the atomic reference cut long-term drift roughly 70x versus the classical sensor alone.
content_html: Satellite navigation is the invisible backbone of modern shipping, and it is also fragile — jammed, spoofed, or simply absent. The fallback, an inertial navigation system, works anywhere but slowly wanders off: it only ever measures acceleration, so tiny errors pile up into kilometres. This experiment demonstrates a third option that gives nothing away and needs no infrastructure: navigate by feeling the shape of Earth's gravity field.
extra_html:
Everitt and colleagues put a quantum gravimeter — an atom interferometer that reads gravity by timing freely falling cold atoms — aboard a 29 m surface vessel, in an ordinary cabin with no environmental stabilisation, and hybridised it with a classical accelerometer for bias stabilisation. Over an 83 km maritime trajectory with GNSS excluded from the entire measurement chain, matching the locally measured gravity to a satellite-derived anomaly map held the inertial solution to nautical-mile-level accuracy instead of letting it drift freely.

The same instrument doubles as a survey tool. Run in a GNSS-referenced mode along coastal routes in seas up to Sea State 4, it agreed with existing gravimetric maps at the milligal level and resolved anomalies down to roughly 300 m along track — about fifty times finer than the satellite map's half-power wavelength. The authors also report the first same-instrument comparison of gimbaled and strapdown mobile quantum gravimetry, finding the two configurations comparable, which matters because strapdown mounting is what makes such a sensor small enough for an autonomous platform.

related.title: Don't Measure the Field, Measure the Answer
related.hook: A single-qubit sensor gives you one bit per measurement. Instead of averaging thousands of them into a number, why not spend the quantum processing on the question you actually asked?

related.title: Syncing Clocks in Orbit Without Trusting GPS
related.hook: Everything from power grids to finance runs on GPS time, and GPS can be spoofed. An entanglement-based link now synchronises clocks and distributes keys at 30 times the Micius rate.

related.title: Universal Gravitation: One Force, Apple to Moon
related.hook: Newton's leap: the same pull that drops an apple also holds the Moon in orbit. Every mass tugs on every other mass, everywhere in the universe.

flashcards.prompt: What is gravity map matching, in one sentence?
flashcards.back_html: You measure the local strength of gravity, compare it against a pre-existing map of gravity anomalies, and use the match to work out where you are — no satellites, no signals broadcast, nothing to jam.

flashcards.prompt: Why does an inertial navigation system need an external aid like this at all?

choices.text: Its position estimate drifts without correction, since it only integrates measured acceleration
It cannot measure acceleration at all while a vessel is rolling
It stops working entirely once the ship leaves coastal waters

flashcards.explanation_html: An INS builds position by integrating acceleration, so small sensor errors accumulate without bound. Gravity aiding supplies an independent fix that bounds that drift.

flashcards.prompt: What did the atomic sensor add over the classical accelerometer it was paired with?

choices.text: A stable long-term reference — about 70x less drift over a 56-hour test
A much faster sampling rate for tracking wave motion
Immunity to the ship's roll and pitch

flashcards.explanation_html: Atom interferometry ties the measurement to atomic constants rather than a drifting mechanical spring, so it anchors the classical channel's bias over long runs.
